content: Annual ryegrass toxicity (ARGT) is a condition that results in the poisoning of livestock due to the presence of a toxin in annual ryegrass that has been infected by a specific bacterium. This toxin is produced by the bacterium Rathayibacter toxicus, which was previously known as Clavibacter toxicus. The bacterium is introduced into the ryegrass by a nematode species called Anguina funesta. The first documented cases of ARGT occurred in the 1950s in the Black Springs region of South Australia. By the 1960s, the disease had also been identified in the Gnowangerup region of Western Australia. Since then, the disease has spread extensively, and it is now estimated that between 40,000 and 60,000 square kilometers of farmland in Western Australia, as well as similar areas in South Australia, are affected by the organisms responsible for ARGT. The majority of livestock losses associated with ARGT occur between the months of October and January. However, cases of poisoning have also been reported as late as April. Efforts to mitigate the risk of ARGT have included the application of herbicides to reduce the population of ryegrass. While this approach has been effective in lowering the risk of ARGT, it has also led to undesirable consequences, such as a significant decline in pasture productivity and the development of herbicide resistance in ryegrass populations. A more recent and promising method of controlling ARGT involves the use of a biological control agent known as the twist fungus. This fungus has been shown to effectively reduce the risk of ARGT without requiring the elimination of ryegrass.
